items.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023
items.q: I said, “Okay, ‘Bolero’ I’ve got it,” and started to play like Ravel’s “Bolero.”

ctx.x: Yeah he was in a very playful mood I think. Have you come across an instance, it could have been for a recording session or maybe a live gig, where you knew you were going to be playing a style and you said oh I’ve never quite done this before? I’m thinking specifically maybe of certain Latin kinds of grooves?

Yeah. I do the same kind of dive deep into research and listen to records that I have or search for records that have the feel that they’re talking about. I remember doing a record with Jon Secada that won a Grammy, I don’t know what year it was, maybe early 90s or something. And I was so embarrassed I put both feet in my mouth when the leader said, “This is ‘Bolero.’” And I said, “Okay, ‘Bolero’ I’ve got it,” and started to play like Ravel’s “Bolero.” He said, na-na-na-na balero. And it’s just a [scats] just a…

the tumba on the conga. You know, the bass drum goes here because, so you’re not in the way of what’s already there. A lot of times a Latin thing, it doesn’t have drums at all, it’s congas and timbales and cowbell and shaker maybe, so to fit the drumset in is a delicate operation. And there’s some guys who do it really well, you know like Richie Morales, I’m thinking of a lot of guys, Vince Cherico is great, plays with Arturo O’Farrill’s big band. It’s a special thing to fit in with the Latin percussion and not…
